E1813.summary: Porphyry's distinction, reported by Atwood, between common death, freeing the body from the soul, and philosophic death, freeing the soul from the body.
E1813.body: Reported from Porphyry: “there is, says he, a twofold death” [II.3 ¶37] — the common death, in which the body is freed from the soul, and the philosophic death, in which the soul is freed from the body. The voice is Porphyry's as cited by Atwood.

E1814.summary: Apostolic ordinances or material signs, such as water, oil, salt and light, which Atwood says signified real efficacies but later became a source of dissension.
E1814.body: Atwood says that in apostolic practice “certain ordinances and elementary types, as of water, oil, salt and light, signified some real and notable efficacies” [I.1 ¶26]. She also calls them material signs, and says that “these very shadows and types of doctrines” became a source of dissension [I.1 ¶26].

E1815.summary: In the Osiris fable, the brother who kills and scatters Osiris; applied to the work, the wrathful fire or Efficient of dissolution, and the unclean Instrument that putrefies the gold.
E1815.body:
In Atwood's reading of the fable, Typhon is Osiris's uterine brother, who kills and scatters him. Applied to the work, he is the wrathful fire or Efficient of the dissolution, and also a name for the unclean Instrument that moves the gold to putrefy. Isis gradually enthrals him [III.1 ¶63].

Asserted identities:
- The adepts' names: “Adepts call him the Green Lion, Typhon, Firedrake”. And “or during the mortification, he is their venomous Black Toad” [III.1 ¶56].
- As the Instrument moving the gold to putrefy: “it is called by them Typhon, Satan, Aquafoetida, Ignis Gehanna, Mortis Immundities, etc.” [III.1 ¶61].
- “they gave to Typhon, in this predicament, the name of Seth, Bebo” [III.1 ¶63]. These names import “a certain violent, forcible restraint, contrariety, and subversion” [III.1 ¶63].

Atwood presents these as the adepts' names, set out in her own exposition.

E1816.summary: The state reached by passing through reason and beyond every bound, which Atwood identifies with the Infinity of Life.
E1816.body: Atwood describes it as the state reached by passing through reason beyond every bound: “that kind of ultimate ignorance, which is the Infinity of Life” [III.2 ¶54]. She equates it with the Infinity of Life.

E1817.summary: An unattributed saying that Atwood cites to show the promise that God may be found, though he remains hidden.
E1817.body: Atwood cites “Seek and ye shall find, knock and it shall be opened unto you” without attribution [II.1 ¶26]. She uses it to illustrate the promise that God may be found, though he remains hidden.

E1818.summary: An unattributed declaration that Atwood introduces with “as is declared”, cited in support of the purged life flowing forth as a panacea.
E1818.body: Introduced only with “as is declared”, the phrase “a pure panacea from the god of Light” [III.1 ¶10] supports Atwood's point that the purged life flows forth as a panacea.

E1819.summary: An unattributed saying, introduced with “as we are abundantly instructed”, cited in support of dissolving the Vital Spirit's natural bind.
E1819.body: Atwood introduces it only with “as we are abundantly instructed”: “Flesh and blood cannot enter into the kingdom of heaven, neither doth corruption inherit corruption” [III.2 ¶62]. She cites it in support of dissolving the natural bind of the Vital Spirit. The text gives no attribution.

E1820.summary: Unattributed English and Latin couplets that Atwood cites about Art advancing nature, the descent to the Paternal, and finding without seeking.
E1820.body:
Atwood cites three couplets without attribution:
- On the descent undertaken to reach the Paternal: “To find the Hero, for whose only sake We sought the dark abodes and crossed the bitter lake.” [II.4 ¶24].
- In Latin, on finding that comes without seeking: “Quaeres multum et non invenies; Fortasse invneies cumnon quaeres.” [III.2 ¶58]. Our rendering (by: ours): You will seek much and not find; perhaps you will find when you do not seek.
- In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), in support of alchemy advancing nature beyond her created state: “Art, then, what nature left in hand doth take, And out of one a twofold work doth make.” [APP ¶156].

E1821.summary: An unattributed Latin tag, “Visitabis interiore terrae”, appended to the Appendix's account of successive dissolutions.
E1821.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), the tag “Visitabis interiore terrae, etc.” [APP ¶182] is appended to the account of successive dissolutions. Our rendering (by: ours): You will visit the interior of the earth. It is given as a reference only, without comment.

E1822.summary: Unattributed Latin verses that Atwood cites to illustrate the ascent, return to the archetypal world, illumination, the four principles and knowledge of God.
E1822.body:
Atwood cites many Latin verses without attribution (all renderings below are ours):
- “Non levis adscensus, si quis petat ardua, sudor” (no light toil is the ascent, if one seeks the heights), on the toil of the ascent [II.2 ¶30].
- “Ille deum vitam accipiet, divisque videbit” (he shall receive the life of the gods, and shall see [among] the gods), on attaining the life of the gods [II.4 ¶51].
- “Tunc ire ad mundum archetypum saepe atque redire” (then to go often to the archetypal world and return), on repeated going to and returning from the archetypal world [II.4 ¶53, II.4 ¶54].
- “Si tu, Deus meus, illuminaveris me Lux fiunt tenebrae meae.” (If you, my God, illumine me, my darkness becomes light), on darkness made light [III.2 ¶11].
- “Mundum mente gerens, similique in imagine formas” (bearing the world in mind, and forming [it] in a like image), on the world being formed after a supernal exemplar held in mind. It carries footnote (27) [III.3 ¶39, III.3 ¶40].
- “Janua clausa est, vah quae lamentabilis haec vox;” (the door is shut, alas, what a lamentable cry), on the shut door that hands cannot force [IV.1 ¶38].
- “Primus dicatur in quo sensus dominatur.” (let that be called first in which sense rules), on the four principles and their relations, graded against the senses [IV.2 ¶10].
- “Nec Sentire Deum nisi qui pars ipse Dei sit.” (nor does any perceive God unless he himself be part of God), in support of the point that only what is part of God perceives God [IV.2 ¶42].
- In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer): “Felix qui potuit rerum cognoscere causas” (happy he who could know the causes of things). There it is called a grand declaration of a deep Hermetic truth: the light of life, lodged in its causal center, frees the threefold life [APP ¶148, APP ¶149, APP ¶150].

E1823.summary: An unattributed Latin maxim, “Ne tu augeas fatum”, that Atwood renders “Enlarge not thy destiny” as a warning to the would-be practitioner.
E1823.body: Atwood cites “Ne tu augeas fatum” [IV.3 ¶56] with the English “Enlarge not thy destiny” (by: book). She uses it to warn the would-be practitioner against presumption.

E1824.summary: Unattributed quotations that Atwood uses for the dreamlike nature of human beings and to name the magic earth.
E1824.body: Atwood quotes “such stuff as dreams are made of” [III.2 ¶7] to illustrate the dreamlike nature of human beings, set against the real discovery of the Matter. She also quotes “Land of Havilah, where good gold is” [III.2 ¶8] to identify the magic earth.

E1825.summary: Unattributed sayings that Atwood cites about the fear of God as the beginning of wisdom and about the seeker giving up his riches.
E1825.body: In a footnote, Atwood cites “The fear of God is the beginning of wisdom, and the knowledge of the Holy is understanding” [I.3 n19]. It supports the admonition to fear God, which she says is proved in alchemy. In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), “The ransom of a man’s life are his riches” [APP ¶158] supports the point that the seeker gives up the riches set before him.

E1826.summary: An unattributed scriptural phrase cited in the Appendix to support the point that the Fall accords with a purpose of greater restoration.
E1826.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), the phrase “eternal purpose, purposed in Christ Jesus, our Lord” [APP ¶98] supports the view that the Fall accords with a purpose of greater restoration.

E1827.summary: Unattributed English verses that Atwood cites about alchemy's concrete evidence, the invisible matter, the divine mover, Saturn bound, the working-place, perseverance and the reign of Mind.
E1827.body:
Atwood cites many verses without attribution:
- The evidence of alchemy was concrete, not “vaguely opinable, But clean, experimental and determinable” [I.1 ¶78].
- The heavenly bodies proclaim a divine mover: “"The Hand that moves us is divine".” [II.4 ¶30].
- The material of the Magistry is invisible and insensible: “A nature to search out which is invisible,” [III.1 ¶7].
- “Saturn, with honey of the bees produced, Sunk in ebriety; fast bind the god.” [III.1 ¶67, III.1 ¶68]. Atwood glosses this as Intellect cutting off the sated Saturnian Will.
- The need for a fitting working-place: “It is a grace - To finde a fitting working-place.” [III.4 ¶43].
- Persevering, with the completed work kept in mind as aim and model: “Begin today, nor end till evil sink In its due grave” [IV.3 ¶51].
- The hoped-for reign of Mind and man's second birth: “Then shall the reign of Mind commence on earth” [IV.3 ¶52, IV.3 ¶53].
- The divine faculty is confined from birth, yet light can enter: “The beams pour in, and truth and skill may couch the blind.” [IV.4 ¶16].

E1828.summary: An unattributed verse about Helius, cited to illustrate the descent to the realm of night and the ancestors, which leads into the discussion of Aeneas.
E1828.body: The verse “To Erebus he went, and the sad realms of night” [II.4 ¶19, II.4 ¶20] is cited without attribution. It concerns Helius and illustrates the descent to the realm of night and the ancestors, leading into Atwood's discussion of Aeneas.

E1829.summary: An unattributed verse on Proteus that Atwood cites to illustrate the one omniform subject.
E1829.body: Atwood cites a verse on Proteus, “Etherial, watery, earthy general soul, Immortal Fire!” [I.2 ¶34, I.2 ¶35], without attribution. She uses it to illustrate the one omniform subject.

forms: unattributed words: 'the fear of the Lord is the beginning of Wisdom'
the fear of the Lord is the beginning of Wisdom
E1830.summary: An unattributed saying whose meaning, the Appendix says, becomes clear on contact with universal power, the initial of regenerate life.
E1830.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), the words “the fear of the Lord is the beginning of Wisdom” [APP ¶175] are said to become clear in meaning on contact with universal power, the initial of regenerate life.

E1831.summary: The human understanding, taken as an essence to be purified, whose occult Causality can be developed to consciousness.
E1831.body: Atwood speaks of “purifying the human Understanding Essence, and developing to consciousness its occult Causality” [II.2 ¶22]. In her usage it is the human understanding, considered as an essence that must be purified and that holds a hidden causality able to become conscious.

E1832.summary: The light that, Atwood says, the Divine Law takes from the spirit while it is in full vigour, so as to give it a motive.
E1832.body: Atwood says the Divine Law deprives the spirit “when in full vigor of its Understanding Light” [III.1 ¶28]. She says this is done to give the spirit a motive.

E1833.summary: The human understanding, which mystical exercises and preparations bring into contact with its Antecedent Cause, in a view Atwood reports from Aristotle.
E1833.body: In a view Atwood reports from Aristotle, mystical exercises and preparations bring it about that “the human Understanding Medium is made to pass into contact with its Antecedent Cause” [II.1 ¶37].

E1834.summary: The higher spirit that, once false imagination is destroyed, can superinduce Divinity, rise above nature, and be inducted by the Mysteries to its Source.
E1834.body: In Atwood's voice, false imagination must be destroyed “before the understanding spirit can superinduce Divinity” [II.2 ¶10]. The trials go on “till the Understanding Spirit rises superior to the dominion of nature” [II.2 ¶13]. The Mysteries were “real inductions of the Understanding Spirit to its Source” [IV.4 ¶5]. In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), a graven image is “carved into the understanding spirit which conceives it by the desire of life” [APP ¶100]. There it is also that of which the connate spirit may be deprived.

E1835.summary: What is nourished and educated in the Elysian state as the embryo life unfolds.
E1835.body: Atwood speaks of “the nourishment and education of the understanding vehicle” [II.4 ¶16]. This takes place in the Elysian state as the embryo life unfolds.

E1836.summary: Atwood's name for the subject of the Hermetic art, referred to as “her”, which the art takes where nature leaves it and then disposes and manipulates.
E1836.body: Atwood calls the subject of the art “this our Undetermined Subject” and refers to it as “her”. The art takes it where nature leaves it and undertakes “the right disposition and manipulation of this our Undetermined Subject” [II.2 ¶27].

E1837.summary: In Hermes as Atwood cites him, the temperate unguent is fire, and unguents are called sulphurs. The true unguent is occult, buried in the matter's own body, and extracted without combustion.
E1837.body:
These are Hermes's words as Atwood cites them. “The temperate unguent, which is fire” [I.3 ¶24] is the medium between faeces and water and the Perscrutinator of the water. “For the unguents are called sulphurs” [I.3 ¶24], because fire, oil and sulphur are closely akin. So unguent = fire = sulphurs.

The true unguent is “the occult and buried unguent” [I.3 ¶54]. It lies in the matter's own body and is the Form of all other unguents. It has no apparent preparation and is extracted without combustion. It is distinct from unguents made of fats, hair and the like. Hermes also says “the ointments which contain the tincture coagulate the tincture, coagulate the fugitive and adorn the sulphurs” [I.3 ¶54].

E1838.summary: The condition in which alone, Atwood says, immortality is consummated; also the joining of the line's end with its beginning, which is Eternity rather than time.
E1838.body: Atwood writes that “immortality is only to be consummated in union” [IV.3 ¶58]. On the joining of the line's end with its beginning, she says: “they join not in time, for their union is Eternity” [IV.3 ¶62]. So union = Eternity.

E1839.summary: Apparently the soul's last remaining unity, about which it rallies as it draws back from nonentity.
E1839.body: The soul, drawing back from nonentity, is described as “rallying about her last deserted Unit” [III.2 ¶55]. Apparently this is the soul's last remaining unity. The voice of the passage is unclear.

E1840.summary: The inseparable unity at which the reiterated analysis finally arrives.
E1840.body: Atwood says the reiterated analysis goes on “until it arrives at the inseparable Unit of Truth” [IV.1 ¶20].

E1841.summary: The whole, identified with the Kingdom of God, which must be sought before any finite end, and into which one returns by abandoning selfhood.
E1841.body: Atwood speaks of “returning again, however, into the Universal and abandoning the selfhood” [IV.4 ¶27]. The Universal is the whole: one ceases to be it by becoming dividual and returns into it by giving up selfhood. In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), it must be sought before any finite end, and it is equated with the Kingdom of God: “before you seek the Universal --- the Kingdom of God” [APP ¶135].

E1842.summary: The occult being in nature on whose assumption, Atwood says, the whole of Hermetic theory and practice proceeds.
E1842.body: Atwood states that “the whole of the Hermetic theory and practice proceeds upon the assumption of a certain Universal Being in nature, which is occult” [I.2 ¶26].
